explanations.explanation: Twelve it is, baker. Luke says that when He was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the Feast. So this trip is the same yearly trip, just with a twelve-year-old along. I bet that detail matters, because it's the age where this whole story happens.

Eight is a fair guess, but the text gives a different number. Luke says Jesus was twelve years old on this trip. The family had been going every year, so this wasn't a first visit. This was just the year things got interesting.

Thirty is the age Luke gives later, when Jesus begins His ministry (Luke 3:23). That's a whole lot of years down the road from this scene. Here, Luke says He was twelve years old. So picture a boy, not a grown man, standing in the middle of all this.
Close, but the text says the opposite. Luke writes that His parents were unaware He had stayed. They headed for home thinking everything was fine. That's the whole reason the search starts later.

Right, baker. Luke says the boy Jesus remained behind in Jerusalem, but His parents were unaware He had stayed. They set off for home with no idea. I've lost track of a cookie or two on the cooling rack, but never a whole twelve-year-old!

Yes, that's where they start. Luke says they traveled on for a day before they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends. They had been assuming He was in their company. So the first search is a walk down the line of people they know.

Priests and Levites aren't mentioned anywhere in this part of the story. Luke says they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends. That was the first place they checked. It makes sense to start with the people you travel with.
No merchants or traders show up in this scene. Luke says they looked for Him among their relatives and friends. That's the crowd they had been traveling with. The shopping crowd never gets a mention.

explanations.answer: Go back to Jerusalem to search
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Luke says that when they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him. They had already gone a full day's travel, so that's a long walk back. They didn't stop looking, and that tells you plenty.
Nazareth was their home, but Luke never says they sent word there. The text says they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him. They went back themselves. I think that's what most of us would do too.

explanations.answer: Wait on the road for Him
explanations.explanation: Waiting sounds calm, but Luke doesn't say they did that. When they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him. They went looking rather than sitting still. Later His mother says they had been anxiously searching (Luke 2:48), so sitting still doesn't fit.
Three, baker. Luke says that finally, after three days, they found Him. The word finally is right there in the verse. I think every one of those days felt long to them.
Seven days would be a longer search than the one Luke describes. The text says that after three days they found Him. Three days of searching is plenty already. So hold on to that number three.
Forty is a big number, and a lot of Bible stories use it, but this isn't one of them. Luke says they found Him after three days. That's how long the search lasted. It was long enough, believe me.

Yes, the temple courts. Luke says they found Him there, sitting among the teachers. After searching all that time, it's the place the search ends. And the boy they'd been searching for was sitting right there in the middle of the conversation.

The Pool of Bethesda is a real place in Jerusalem (John 5:2), but it's not where this story ends up. Luke says they found Him in the temple courts. That's where the teachers were sitting. So the answer is the temple, not the pool.

The Mount of Olives is a real hill near Jerusalem, but Luke doesn't send anyone there in this story. He says they found Him in the temple courts. He was sitting among the teachers. That's the spot where the search finally ends.

Right, baker. Luke says He was sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. Nothing in the text says He was lecturing. Listening and asking is all it says. And yet verse 47 says everyone who heard Him was astounded.

explanations.answer: Reading a scroll aloud to them
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't mention a scroll in this scene. He says Jesus was listening to the teachers and asking them questions. That's all the text tells us about what He was doing. It's a quieter picture than reading aloud.

explanations.answer: Leading them all in a psalm
explanations.explanation: A psalm sounds like it could fit, but Luke doesn't say it. The text says He was sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. He wasn't up front leading anything. He was in the middle of the conversation.
Astounded is the word. Luke says that all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. Notice it says all. Nobody in earshot walked away unimpressed.
Puzzled is close to the mood, but it isn't Luke's word. He says all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. Astounded is a bigger reaction than puzzled. They were amazed.
Annoyed isn't in this scene at all. Luke says that all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. Nobody sighed and checked their watch. They were amazed.

That's it, baker. Jesus asks, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” His parents had been looking for Him, and He answers with a question of His own. It's a statement worth slowing down for.

Nazareth comes next, but it isn't where Jesus says He had to be. Luke says that after this He went down to Nazareth with them. Here He asks, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” So the answer is His Father's house.
The wilderness isn't part of this scene. Jesus says, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” That's the place He names. It was the temple courts where His parents found Him.

That's what you'd expect, but Luke says something different. He writes, “But they did not understand the statement He was making to them.” So His parents heard Him and still didn't follow what He meant. I think that's a very human moment.

Right, baker. Luke says, “But they did not understand the statement He was making to them.” They heard every word and still couldn't connect it. I've nodded along to plenty of directions I didn't follow, so I get it.
True, baker. Luke says that Jesus went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. After the temple, He went home with His parents. That's how the story winds down.
Luke says the opposite. He writes that Jesus went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. Even after the temple scene, He went home with His parents. Obedient is the word the text uses.
Treasures, baker. Luke says, “…treasured up all these things in her heart.” She didn't forget any of it. I think she kept it close, the way you'd hold onto your favorite recipe card.

Fear is a natural guess after three days of searching, but it isn't Luke's word. He says His mother “…treasured up all these things in her heart.” Treasured means she held onto them as precious. She kept them close.
Doubts don't show up in this verse. Luke says His mother “…treasured up all these things in her heart.” She kept everything that happened close to her. So treasures is the word.
That's it, baker. Luke says that Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man. He grew in how He was seen by God and by people. That's how this story ends.
Kings and priests don't appear in this verse. Luke says Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man. Man here means people in general, not one group. And God comes first.

Jews and Greeks are a pairing you see elsewhere in the New Testament, but not in this verse. Luke says Jesus grew in favor with God and man. That's the pair the text gives. So the answer is God and man.
